analysis.one_liner: Bars investors from suing companies over securities fraud in state courts, forcing all such cases into federal court.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee for a year and a half and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the federal securities laws to prohibit investors from bringing private fraud lawsuits in state courts or under state law when the stock in question is a federally registered security. Federal district courts would have exclusive jurisdiction over these cases. State-law fraud claims, including claims attached to federal lawsuits, would be wiped out, leaving only the federal cause of action.
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded companies, underwriters, and other defendants in securities fraud suits gain: they would face lawsuits only in federal court under federal law, eliminating state-court class actions and state-law claims that can offer different and sometimes broader remedies.

how_it_helps.text: It bars any private civil action in state court or under state law alleging misrepresentation, omission, or manipulative or deceptive conduct in the purchase or sale of a covered security.
It grants federal district courts exclusive jurisdiction over suits under the securities laws, ending the concurrent state-court jurisdiction that existed under the Securities Act of 1933.
Supporters describe the goal as uniform national standards for federally registered securities, so the same rules apply in every state rather than varying state-by-state.

analysis.who_pays: Investors who are defrauded would lose the option of suing in state courts or under state law, including state claims joined to federal cases, narrowing the remedies available to them.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates state-law remedies entirely for claims involving federally registered securities, removing legal avenues investors in those states currently have.
Even state claims brought alongside a federal lawsuit would be barred, so plaintiffs could not preserve state-law theories in federal court either.

The fair argument for the bill is that a single federal standard avoids inconsistent state rules and forum shopping for friendlier state courts; the honest cost is that uniformity comes at the price of shutting off state remedies that fraud victims may rely on when federal law's requirements are harder to meet.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Uniform national rules for federally registered securities are a legitimate goal, and defendants have a real complaint about inconsistent state-court suits. But the bill's effect is one-directional: it takes away remedies from defrauded investors and gives defendants protection from state-court litigation, with nothing in the bill strengthening federal remedies in exchange. For ordinary shareholders, the costs outweigh the uniformity benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Finance and Hazardous Materials subcommittee, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Tom Campbell introduced the bill in the House on May 16, 1997.
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the same day.
On May 21, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials.
The bill saw no further action; it never reached a committee markup or a floor vote and died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, investors kept the ability to bring fraud claims in state courts and under state law, and companies facing investor suits did not get the shield the bill would have provided. Had it passed, defendants in securities litigation would have been the main winners.

for.name: Rep. Tom Campbell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors.

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or sent it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a small bipartisan roster of cosponsors, five Republicans and one Democrat, but no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of broader support and opposition was never shown.

industries.industry: Publicly traded companies and securities issuers
industries.note: The bill would shield issuers of federally registered securities from state-court and state-law fraud suits, leaving investors with only the federal cause of action. The industry's gain comes directly out of defrauded investors' ability to recover.

industries.industry: Securities plaintiffs' attorneys and state courts
industries.note: State-court securities fraud litigation, including class actions brought under state law, would be barred for covered securities, and state courts would lose concurrent jurisdiction. Their loss is investors' loss of a forum.
